Executive Summary

The full picture at a glance.

The City of Riverton manages parking enforcement through a legacy system with no real-time integration across its Parking, Finance, IT, and Public Safety departments. Every permit update travels a five-step manual relay: paper form, spreadsheet entry, nightly batch upload, printed officer list, and field enforcement. The average time for a permit change to reach an enforcement officer is 20.7 days.

Analysis of a synthetic dataset of 1,000 records reveals the consequences: 300 incorrect citations (30%), 517 records requiring manual entry (51.7%), 305 resident complaints, and $40,386 in fines waived due to citation errors against a total fine pool of $108,705.

Team 8 proposes a centralized Smart Parking Management System demonstrated through a four-role HTML prototype. The solution eliminates the batch process, replaces manual entry with digital workflows, and gives officers instant permit verification. Simulated future-state data projects a 95% reduction in citation errors, 100% elimination of manual entry, and recovery of $37,186 in currently waived revenue.

Root Cause

Nightly batch processing creates a 20.7-day data lag between permit issuance and officer visibility.

Evidence

1,000-record synthetic dataset generated in Python, visualized through Chart.js and Power BI dashboards.

Solution

Centralized real-time platform with four role-based interfaces, eliminating all manual relay steps.

02  ·  Problem Context & Stakeholders

A broken relay chain harms everyone.

Riverton operates three disconnected legacy systems — Enforcement (345 records), Permit (331), and Finance (324) — none communicating in real time. Every permit update travels a five-step manual process before reaching an officer.

Stakeholders — click to expand

🏠Residents305 appeals▼

305 appeals were filed against incorrect citations in the dataset period. Residents have no digital channel to check permit status or file disputes. Every interaction requires an in-person office visit or phone call. This population bears the direct cost of the system failure in wasted time, stress, and wrongful fines.

🚚Enforcement Officers20.7d lag▼

Officers issue citations using printed permit lists that are on average 20.7 days out of date. They have no tool to verify permit status in real time. This is a process failure, not a personnel failure. Officers are performing their roles correctly within a system that provides them with stale information.

📋Permit Office Staff51.7% manual▼

Over half of all permit records require manual data entry at some point in the processing chain. Each manual entry is a potential source of transcription error. Staff also spend significant time fielding resident complaints and correcting citation records that flow from those errors.

💰Finance Department$40,386 waived▼

Of the $108,705 in fines issued, only $33,672 has been collected. $34,647 remains pending and $40,386 has been waived because citations were wrong. 37% of total fine value was forfeited. Finance cannot reconcile revenue in real time across three disconnected systems.

🏛️City LeadershipNo real-time view▼

Leadership depends on weekly batch reports that do not reflect current conditions. There is no real-time dashboard for permit status, citation volume, or revenue performance. This limits the ability to respond proactively to zone-level error spikes or staffing issues.

03  ·  Research & Insights

What the literature confirms.

Academic research and municipal benchmarks validate every finding in the Riverton dataset. The problem is not unique to Riverton. Batch-processing architectures produce these outcomes systematically across comparable municipalities.

ICMA (2022)

Citation dispute rates 3 to 5 times higher in batch systems

Municipalities using nightly batch processing experience citation error rates consistent with Riverton's 30%. Real-time integration reduces dispute rates 30 to 40% in the first year of deployment.

LaValle et al. (2011)  ·  MIT Sloan

Even incremental data accessibility improvements produce measurable outcomes

Moving from overnight to near-real-time data synchronization produces significant reductions in downstream decision errors. The 20.7-day lag in Riverton is the predictable output of a batch architecture applied to time-sensitive enforcement data.

Davenport & Harris (2007)

Manual entry error rates 8 to 10 times higher than automated capture

With 51.7% of Riverton's records requiring manual entry, the system structurally encodes a high floor of inaccuracy regardless of staff diligence. Digital intake at the point of permit issuance is the only reliable path to data quality.

Laudon & Laudon (2020)

Cloud platforms eliminate on-premise overhead at low marginal cost

Cloud-hosted platforms with role-based access controls provide the infrastructure needed for mobile-first enforcement tools without significant hardware investment. This is the primary technology rationale for the proposed architecture.

05  ·  Dashboard Insights

What Dataset 1 told us.

Finding 01

The 20.7-day lag is the root cause

Every wrong citation, complaint, and waived fine traces to one decision: overnight batch processing. 20.7 days average delay between permit issuance and officer visibility.

Finding 02

51.7% manual entry is a structural risk

Over half the database enters through human transcription. 517 of 1,000 records carry the risk of error before they even reach the batch upload step.

Finding 03

300 wrong citations are a system failure

Officers acted correctly on information that was three weeks old. 30% of all citations issued against valid permits. Not a personnel failure.

Finding 04

Zone Z5 is the critical hotspot

220 records, 71 wrong citations, 115 manual entries. Zone Z5 is highest on every problem metric. First pilot zone for any rollout.

Finding 05

$40,386 is a recoverable annual loss

37% of total fines were waived because citations were wrong. $40,386 is a direct, measurable, and preventable cost.

Finding 06

Three systems, zero shared truth

Enforcement (345), Permit (331), Finance (324) each hold separate records. No master database means every discrepancy is a potential error.

09  ·  Ethical & Social Considerations

Technology with responsibility.

A centralized system handling municipal data carries real responsibilities. These considerations were embedded in the design from the start, not added as an afterthought.

🔒

Data Privacy

The system handles personally identifiable information including resident names, vehicle registration data, payment history, and citation records. Role-based access controls limit data visibility strictly by function. Enforcement officers see only permit status, not full resident profiles. All data must be encrypted at rest and in transit under applicable municipal data governance frameworks.

⚖️

Algorithmic Fairness

Zone Z5 appears most heavily in the dataset due to data lag patterns in the current system, not resident behavior. Any future predictive enforcement model built on historical data risks encoding this bias. The distinction between system-caused error concentrations and genuine behavioral patterns must be preserved in model design and documentation.

🌐

Digital Equity

Moving permit applications and dispute filing online disadvantages residents without reliable internet access or digital literacy. The implementation must maintain analog fallback channels — phone and in-person service — and provide digital literacy support, particularly in higher-density zones like Z5 where the problem impact is already disproportionate.

🌿

Environmental Benefit

Eliminating paper permit forms, printed officer lists, and manual filing processes produces a measurable reduction in paper consumption. This aligns with municipal sustainability commitments and represents a low-cost co-benefit of the modernization effort that can be quantified and reported alongside the operational KPIs.

10  ·  Lessons Learned & Team Reflection

What the process taught us.

Most Important Decision

Accurate language matters more than impressive language

Early deliverables described AWS Lambda, AWS RDS, and AWS QuickSight as built components. These were proposed elements, not delivered ones. The mid-project correction — relabeling the HTML prototype, Chart.js visualizations, and Power BI dashboard accurately — enforced the most important principle of the project: solution language must reflect what was built, not what was planned.

Key Takeaway

Synthetic data generation requires deep domain understanding

Defining a realistic synchronization lag distribution, fine amount range, and zone-level incorrect citation rates forced analytical engagement with the problem domain before writing a single line of code. The decision to model Zone Z5 as the highest-impact zone was derived from the insight that higher record counts and more frequent permit changes produce wider lag windows in batch systems.

Team Dynamics

Role clarity across five people was the foundation of delivery

The Project Manager maintained document consistency and coordinated the mid-project correction across all deliverables simultaneously. The IT Architect led prototype development. The Dashboard Developer built Power BI visualizations. The Business Process Analyst and Data Analyst developed the DPAD and data analysis narrative. Assignments stayed clear even as deliverables iterated and deadlines shifted.

Transferable Principle

Internal traceability is what makes a project defensible

Every figure across every deliverable — 20.7 days, 51.7%, $40,386, 305 complaints, $108,705 total fines — appears consistently across both dashboards, the KPI document, and the written report. This consistency is what makes the project coherent as a portfolio piece and defensible under academic and professional scrutiny.

From fragmented to unified.

Riverton's parking operations suffer from one architectural decision. A nightly batch process keeps departments 20 days apart. The proposed centralized system eliminates that gap, and with it, nearly every downstream problem.
